passages.original: sed unus sit Deus,tecum disputare non debeo ; quia nisi credideris, intelligere nullatenus poteris. Et tamen Filium Dei Deum 1 fatetur Mercurius. Hoc lapide percussus, lapideus desinat esse sacrilepus, Audiamus quid etiam Sibylla vates eorum de codem dicat: Alium, inquit, dedit Deus filiis irominum 2 colendum. Quantum apparet, in his sententii!; Mercurii etSibylla, Sabellius etiam judicatur. Mercurius et Patrem Deum dicit et Filium : ct Sibylla dicit Deum alium.
passages.english: but that God is one, I ought not to argue with you, because unless you believe, you will by no means be able to understand. And yet Mercury confesses the Son of God [to be] God. Struck by this stone, let the sacrilegious man cease to be [made] of stone. Let us hear also what the Sibyl, their prophetess, says about the same: "God," she says, "gave another to the sons of men to be worshipped." As far as appears, in these sayings of Mercury and the Sibyl, Sabellius too is judged. Mercury calls both the Father God and the Son, and the Sibyl says "another God."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence (the preceding words are "how God is Father, and the Son God, and yet not two gods"). Scanning errors corrected: "sacrilepus" read as sacrilegus, "codem" as eodem, "irominum" as hominum, "sententii!;" as sententiis, "ct" as et; the digits 1 and 2 are footnote marks. "Mercury" is Hermes Trismegistus. "Deum alium" may also be construed "another [as] God."

It begins mid-sentence, continuing "With Gregory on the Gospels, homily 53", and it breaks off mid-sentence before the quoted verse.
